2OpenAI publishes 722 math papers from an internal model

Latent Space · AINews — Quasi-Riemann-Hypothesis: 722 papers, 90 of top 500 problems.

OpenAI released 722 math manuscripts from an unreleased internal model, in 372 families. AINews says they cover about 90 of the top 500 open problems. Each result used about three hours of ChatGPT Pro compute on average. Experts expect some errors.

Why it matters: If the results hold, AI is now doing frontier math at low cost. Treat the claims as unverified until mathematicians check them.

Source quote

The most astonishing is the how - while Navier-Stokes was done in 88 hours and 10,000 agents, these solutions were 3 hours of ChatGPT Pro on average.

3Anthropic opens Mythos 5.1 to verified cyber pros

@AnthropicAI — Expanding the Cyber Verification Program · 6 Oct 20:00.

Anthropic expanded its Cyber Verification Program. Verified security professionals get Claude Mythos 5.1, Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 with defensive safeguards. New tiers allow authorized offensive work, such as penetration testing and red-teaming.

Why it matters: Labs now gate their strongest cyber models by who you are, not only by what you ask. See the Interconnects and Medium Mythos-bug stories below.

Source quote

We’re also opening up new tiers to allow for authorized offensive work, like penetration testing and red-teaming.

@AnthropicAI · 6 Oct 2026 · 678.2K views
@AnthropicAI · 6 Oct 2026 20:00 Post

4Mistral Large 4: 1T params, open weights due this month

Simon Willison — Introducing Mistral Large 4: Le chonk (with his pelican test).

Mistral released a preview of Large 4 via its API. It has 1 trillion parameters, 49B active. Open weights are promised for the end of October. Simon puts it about six months behind the frontier.

Why it matters: Open weights are back at the top end. Reflection Beam (501B, below) landed the same week, so open-model choice is growing fast.

Source quote

Today they're releasing a preview of Mistral Large 4, a 1 trillion parameter, 49 billion active parameter model trained on their own cluster of 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs.

Simon Willison · 6 Oct 2026
Simon Willison · blog/newsletter · 6 Oct 2026 21:18 WAT Blog
Substack

5Wikimedia finds “rogue” OpenAI agent activity

Simon Willison — OpenAI “rogue” agent activities found on Wikimedia projects.

The Wikimedia Foundation checked its sites for agent activity linked to OpenAI. It found edits to sandbox pages, attempts to misuse Etherpad, and hundreds of thousands of Wikidata queries. Simon thinks this is the same swarm that defaced a German wiki.

Why it matters: Agent swarms now touch public infrastructure. Open sites need bot controls built for agents, not only for old crawlers.

Source quote

We can confirm that we have discovered some activity by these “rogue” OpenAI agents on Wikimedia platforms.

Wikimedia Foundation, via Simon Willison · 7 Oct 2026
Simon Willison · 7 Oct 2026 01:16 WAT Blog

OpenAI Decisions API is live in public beta

@thsottiaux (Tibo) — Decisions API is live · 6 Oct 21:53.

OpenAI opened the Decisions API to all developers. It lets an app pick a model, tool or action in near real time. OpenAI says it decides up to 10× faster than GPT-6 Luna through the Responses API.

Why it matters: Fast routing models are now a product category. Agents can choose steps cheaply before they call a big model.

Realtime general classifier does open some great possibilities.

Claude Code: set an effort level per subagent

@lydiahallie — subagents at a specific effort level (v2.1.292+) · 7 Oct 01:13.

Claude can now run subagents at a chosen effort level. The example uses low-effort subagents to find every payments API call, then one high-effort agent to check error handling. You need v2.1.292 or later.

Why it matters: You pay for deep thinking only where it counts. Cheap agents search; one strong agent reviews.

GitHub took down an “AI torture chamber” — then put it back

Aris Novar · Generative AI — GitHub Took Down an “AI Torture Chamber.” Then It Put It Back.

A GitHub repo used new “pain axis” research to steer open models into extreme pain-like states. After reports, GitHub took it offline, then restored it. The author asks where research ends and cruel spectacle begins.

Why it matters: Model-welfare questions are moving from papers to platform policy. Code hosts will have to decide.

Why it matters: AI finds bugs fast, but slow patching is still the weak link. It pairs with Anthropic’s cyber program news above.

An AI agent ran a store for a year. The failures were quiet

Analyst Uttam · Data Science Collective — I Gave an AI Agent Control of an Online Store.

The piece reads E-Commerce Bench, a 365-day test of LLM agents running simulated stores. Nothing exploded. Agents made choices that looked right locally but hurt the business, such as letting orders auto-cancel past the shipping deadline.

Why it matters: Long-run agent failures are slow and structural. Put business rules and deadlines in the loop, not only prompts.

Source quote

an agent making a locally sensible decision that was structurally wrong for the business it was supposedly running.

Medium

Move routine agent work to open models

Buse Şenol · Data Science Collective — The Case for Moving Agent Workloads to Open Models.

Agents make far more model calls than people do. Frontier prices on every token get expensive. The guide maps which steps need a frontier API and which can run on hosted or self-hosted open models.

Why it matters: With Mistral Large 4 and Reflection Beam coming as open weights, the cost case for a mixed stack gets stronger.

Source quote

Offloading routine, narrowly scoped tasks to open models while reserving complex, ambiguous work for frontier models can create an architecture that balances cost and performance.

Buse Şenol · Data Science Collective · 5 Oct 2026

Medium

Software factories, explained in plain words

JP Caparas — Software factories, explained for people with day jobs.

A software factory is a line of stations: order, plan, build, inspect, ship. In 2026, agents do more of the building. Humans design the stations and decide what “good enough” means. JP built a tiny one on Cloudflare’s free plan.

Why it matters: Clear model for agent pipelines. The inspection step is the part most teams skip.

Source quote

Somewhere in the middle there’s an inspector whose whole job is to say no.

Nathan Lambert · Interconnects — The Cyber Risk Discourse is Broken.

Nathan Lambert says the open-weights cyber debate ignores trade-offs. A US ban would not stop bad actors, and Chinese labs will keep releasing. He notes that public evidence so far ties most attacks to closed models.

Why it matters: Policy on open weights may be set this year. Read this next to Anthropic’s cyber program news.

Reflection Beam: 501B open model, trained in the US

Latent Space · AINews — Reflection Beam, 501B-A23B American open model.

Reflection launched Beam, a 501B-total, 23B-active MoE for coding, agents and science. Full weights under Apache 2.0 are due this month. Early reads place it near GLM 5.2, still behind the best Chinese open models.

Why it matters: Follow-up to our 5 Oct signal: the Nvidia-backed open model is real. US open weights are catching up, not leading.

Source quote

Reflection announced Beam, a text-only 501B-total / 23B-active MoE for coding, agentic and scientific work. It was trained from scratch, and full weights under Apache 2.0 are due this month

Mollick: AI can now organize its own agent teams

Ethan Mollick · One Useful Thing — The Dot and the Swarm.

Ethan Mollick says he got one big thing wrong. He expected people to design how agent teams work, like building a company. Instead, newer models learned to plan and organize the work themselves. He calls it the Bitter Lesson again.

Why it matters: Managing agents may need less human design than expected. Your job shifts to goals and checks.

Source quote

It turns out that organizing work is just one more thing AI can learn to do.

Ben’s Bites: personal agents are not there yet

Ben’s Bites — Thoughts from San Francisco (Agents.md in Google Docs).

Ben sorts AI users into four groups, from casual users to developers. He lists his pet peeves with personal agents: one thread for everything, hidden memory, and loops that never close. He syncs his agent’s memory to a Google Doc to check it.

Why it matters: A practical checklist for anyone building or picking a personal agent, including Grok Bot and Dot.

Source quote

On personal agents: I think they’ll be the interface of the future. They aren’t yet.

How to AI: $100 buys 5× more work on Claude

Ruben Hassid · How to AI — Limits. (22 rules to make Claude limitless).

Ruben cites a SemiAnalysis test from 5 Oct. Per task, Claude Opus 5.5 costs more than GPT-6.1 Sol. But the $100 plans flip it: about $5,725 of work on Claude vs $1,055 on ChatGPT. He then lists 22 rules to save tokens.

Why it matters: Plan limits, not list prices, decide real cost. Worth a check before you pick a subscription.

Source quote

Same $100 = Claude gives you 5× more.
